questions.q: Precisely what does the security_admin role bypass when it's elevated?
options: Only the password policy, with no effect on ACL records at all
ACL script evaluation specifically when editing sys_security_acl records, not ACL enforcement across the rest of the platform
Nothing — security_admin is a label with no actual functional effect
Every ACL on every table for every user, platform-wide, for as long as the admin role is held
questions.explain: The bypass is narrow and specific: it applies to editing ACL records themselves, while every other ACL continues evaluating normally for everyone else.

questions.q: Why is a bad edit made while security_admin is elevated so much more dangerous than a bad edit to an ordinary record?
options: Because ACL edits made under elevation are permanent and can never be reverted
Because elevation also deletes the audit history for every other table automatically
There's no real difference in risk compared to editing any other record
Because ACLs govern what every other role, user, and table can do, so a careless or malicious ACL edit can widen access far beyond the single record being changed
questions.explain: The bypass itself is narrow (ACL record edits), but the consequence is platform-wide, because ACLs are the rules that decide access everywhere else.

questions.q: Why is security_admin deliberately NOT granted permanently alongside the admin role, even for a trusted full administrator?
options: Because leaving that bypass live for every routine admin session would create a wide, mostly-unnecessary window to rewrite platform-wide access rules
Because ServiceNow technically does not allow any role to be held permanently under any configuration
Because admins never actually need to edit ACL records, so the role serves no purpose
Because permanent roles cost more in ServiceNow's licensing model
questions.explain: The vast majority of admin work never touches an ACL record, so scoping the bypass to deliberate, session-based elevation avoids leaving that leverage open by default.

questions.q: What is the real governance practice this lesson emphasizes beyond simply restricting who can elevate to security_admin?
options: Logging every elevation event and alerting on unusual elevation patterns, treating elevation itself as a security-sensitive, auditable moment
Disabling ACLs on sys_security_acl so elevation is never required
Removing the Elevate Roles option from the platform entirely so no one can ever elevate
Granting security_admin to every user so elevation events become unremarkable
questions.explain: Restricting who can elevate solves only half the problem; logging and alerting on the elevation event itself catches misuse even by someone who technically had the right to elevate.

questions.q: What broader question does security_admin's design illustrate about any layered access-control system?
options: Whether encryption at rest is sufficient on its own to secure a platform
Who governs the governors — what stops the mechanism that enforces the rules from being quietly rewritten by someone with just enough access to reach it
Whether role names should be short or long for readability
Whether single sign-on eliminates the need for any role-based access control
questions.explain: security_admin is a concrete answer to that general governance question: scope the bypass narrowly, require deliberate elevation, and audit every use of it.
